entities.summary:
Pope Nicholas II, also known as Gerard of Burgundy, was a pivotal figure in the 11th century, marking a significant shift in the Catholic Church's influence in Italy and the Mediterranean. 

Born into a noble family, Nicholas II rose to prominence as the Bishop of Florence and later became the Pope on January 24, 1059. His papacy, which lasted until his death on July 27, 1061, was characterized by his efforts to consolidate papal power and expand the Church's influence in southern Italy. 

One of Nicholas II's most notable achievements was his role in passing papal election reforms, which restricted the deliberation of candidates to the Cardinal Bishops. This reform had a lasting impact on the development of the papacy and the Catholic Church's governance structure. 

The legacy of Pope Nicholas II can be seen in the continued influence of the Catholic Church in Italy and the Mediterranean region. His reforms also laid the groundwork for future papal efforts to shape European politics and society. 

The passing of Nicholas II marked the end of an era, but his impact on the Catholic Church and the region would be felt for centuries to come.
